items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: MLK's 'I have a dream' was largely improvised
items.claim: On 28 August 1963, King's speech at the Lincoln Memorial included the famous refrain. How did it enter the speech?

options.text: It was the title and central image of the prepared text
The prepared text did not include the dream section — Mahalia Jackson called out 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' and he set his notes aside
He delivered the speech entirely from memory with no notes
The 'dream' lines were added by an aide after delivery

items.reveal:
King had used the 'dream' rhetoric earlier in 1963 (Detroit, June). His Washington text, drafted with Clarence Jones and Stanley Levison, ended differently. About 11 minutes in, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson — sitting behind him — reportedly called out the prompt. The next eight minutes were extemporaneous.

The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom drew around 250,000 people. The Civil Rights Act passed the following year; the Voting Rights Act in 1965.

FBI surveillance of King intensified after the speech. J. Edgar Hoover called him 'the most dangerous Negro' in America.
items.why: The most quoted lines of 20th-century American speech-making were unscripted. Great rhetorical moments are often the product of preparation plus improvisation — not just the written page.
